title: Spooky Coincidences?
beats: Shows odd coincidences: speed of light digits and pyramid latitude, anagrams
Asks: are these coincidences, and why is finding hidden messages so easy and so fun
Plays reversed Armstrong, then reversed Oswald phrase as a possible confession
Says it is a coincidence: any reversed phrase sounds like that, and shows the app so you can try
Phonetic palindrome defined by example: say yes, reversed
Apophenia, then pareidolia, named after faces-in-water examples
Evolution: hearing a threat in a shadow is safer, so pattern-seekers survive
Random iTunes shuffle felt non-random, so Apple made it less random
Dancing Spider-Man seems to sync with any song; actual tempos are shared and he explains why
Selection bias named, with the pyramid number deconstructed: decimal point choice and meters of tolerance
Confirmation bias; Dark Side of the Moon with Wizard of Oz
Law of near enough; probability lever
Walter Summerford struck three times; frame: avid outdoorsman raises odds
Law of truly large numbers; Disney photo coincidence
Lincoln-Kennedy list, then Michael Stevens as seven letters too; 21 pairs found in a contest
Littlewood's law and 1 in 10 to the 3040; unusual day is one with nothing unusual

metrics.misconception: yes: coincidences imply a hidden cause
metrics.brute_force: yes 12:06: lists Lincoln-Kennedy matches and shows he can make one for himself
metrics.examples: about 10; moves from toy cases (reverse speech) to world events and then probabilities
metrics.ending: Frames improbable days as normal via Diaconis line, then a charity outro

principles.1: confirmed: reversed speech, shuffle, Spider-Man dance, birthday song are everyday experiences (1:02 to 5:45)
principles.2: confirmed: five named terms (apophenia, pareidolia, selection bias, confirmation bias, law of near enough) each given after an example
principles.4: partly: odd-seeming stories are given first, then rigor via probability; never a formula until Littlewood at 12:54
principles.5: confirmed: user is invited to try the reversing app (2:14) and listen to clips
principles.6: partly: brute-force is the coincidence list itself at 11:18 to 12:06
principles.7: confirmed: viewer is shown the Oswald reversal then the claim that everyone sounds the same (1:30 to 2:14)
principles.8: partly: the explanations at 6:35 and 12:54 are dense; speech is not slower and the idea rate is slower only because examples are long stories
principles.9: confirmed: spooky first, debunk second repeated for reversed speech, Spider-Man, pyramid, albums, Lincoln
principles.10: confirmed: single phrase, then dance, then a set of world events, then 7 billion people
principles.11: partly: bias terms arrive in order but the Disney and Lincoln stories reuse the same frame
principles.12: confirmed: Hutson, Hand, Radiolab, Skeptical Inquirer, McLuhan, Diaconis
principles.13: confirmed: plain voice throughout with expert books named

new_moves.name: spooky-then-debunk
new_moves.what: Presents a seemingly paranormal case in full strength, then dismantles it with a named bias

new_moves.name: turn-the-method-on-yourself
new_moves.what: Applies the coincidence-finding to his own name so the learner sees how cheap matches are

theory: The structure alternates a convincing coincidence with its deflation, and each deflation attaches a name to a bias. The learner experiences being fooled before being told why, so the terms stick.
velocity: Orchestrator: a spooky-then-debunk playbook where the tutor shows the false pattern before the correction
Eval: terms appear after at least one lived example
Learner model: use the learner's own name or data to generate a personal coincidence
quote: the truly unusual day would be a day where nothing unusual happens.
